storyboard.claim: This is not covert whisper-campaign bullying — it is an immediate physical threat.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie alone in the dark forest, afraid, a harsh light hitting his face from off-screen.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Context beats established the outdoor movie night; this is the moment the physical threat arrives.
storyboard.addedInformation: The contrast drawn here — Julian's covert notes vs. this overt physical confrontation — is the beat's entire claim; the callout names both sides.

storyboard.claim: Eddie and his friends block Auggie and Jack's path — the threat is physical and immediate.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie and Jack stopped on a dark forest path, afraid, unable to move forward.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the flashlight-in-face moment; the threat escalates from a light to a blocked escape.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: Eddie and his unnamed friends are not in the cast; the blocked pair is shown instead.

storyboard.claim: Jack steps in — but so do Amos, Miles, and Henry, which is the remarkable part.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack standing in front of Auggie, arm out protecting him; shield icon signals protection by multiple defenders.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After the blocked path: now the defenders arrive unexpectedly.
storyboard.addedInformation: Amos, Miles, and Henry are not in the cast; Jack represents the group of defenders.

storyboard.claim: These defenders had been Julian's allies all year — the kids who tormented Jack.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Julian smirking in the classroom — the face of the side these kids had been on.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names who these defenders were before — establishing the reversal's weight.
storyboard.addedInformation: Julian is shown as the former leader whose orbit these kids are now breaking from.

storyboard.claim: They physically position themselves as a human shield between the older kids and Auggie.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack reaching/shielding in front of Auggie; the shield icon makes the physical barrier literal.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The who (former Julian allies) is established; now the what (the physical act) lands.
storyboard.addedInformation: Reach action works here because the shield icon is on screen as its subject.

storyboard.claim: Amos physically rams into Eddie so Auggie and Jack can escape.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack and Auggie walking quickly away through dark pines while the confrontation happens behind them.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The defenders positioned themselves; now one acts — creating the escape path.
storyboard.addedInformation: Amos and Eddie are not in the cast; Jack and Auggie's escape is shown as the result of the intervention.

callout.text: SOCIAL ORDER WAIT YOU DONT THINK

storyboard.claim: This is not a sudden sentimental redemption arc — it has a sociological explanation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie neutral on a stage-analysis frame; the strike callout rejects the 'movie moment' reading.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After the escape: the hosts step back to explain what actually happened.
storyboard.addedInformation: Strike style is used because the narrator explicitly rejects the cliché interpretation.

storyboard.claim: For the whole year the social tension was internal — Julian against Auggie.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Julian pointing at Auggie across the classroom — the year-long internal conflict made visible.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets up the sociology: internal tension all year, about to contrast with external threat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Twoshot framing clarifies the two-sided internal dynamic before the external pivot.

storyboard.claim: When an outside predator attacks, tribal boundaries instantly redraw around the real in-group.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Flow diagram: 'external threat' causes 'tribe redraws' — the sociology engine made visible.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Internal-tension frame (247) pivots to the external-threat mechanism.
storyboard.addedInformation: This is the structural beat; the diagram replaces a callout and captures the causal arrow the narrator states.

storyboard.claim: In that split second the defenders recognize Auggie as a Beecher Prep kid — one of their own.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie surprised in the forest — the moment of recognized belonging.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The flow diagram explained the mechanism; now the human result of that mechanism lands.
storyboard.addedInformation: The older kids' cruelty is described as the catalyst; the callout names the recognition it forced.

storyboard.claim: By defending Auggie, the former Julian allies finally pass the moral test — loyalty over prejudice.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack and Auggie together in the forest; Jack's genuine happiness signals the loyalty is real, not performed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Recognition (249) leads to the moral verdict: they pass the test.
storyboard.addedInformation: Happy on Jack is genuine warmth here — the defenders made the right choice, and it shows.

callout.text: August is no longer the outsider

storyboard.claim: When they return to the group the entire dynamic has shifted — Auggie is no longer marked as 'other.'
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie happy in the classroom — finally himself among peers, the social plague lifted.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The test is passed (250); now the consequence lands in the wider school group.
storyboard.addedInformation: The narrator's phrase 'the plague is dead' is the claim; 'August is just August' is its concrete expression.

storyboard.claim: The social sorting the whole book built around Auggie is now complete.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Sorter diagram: the three columns — with August, against August, neutral — the ledger that closes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Narrative arc closes; the hosts signal a pivot to critical analysis.
storyboard.addedInformation: The sorter mirrors Charlotte's looseleaf paper — it lands as a visual summary before the critical section.

callout.text: He tested everyone in the book

storyboard.claim: Auggie's presence was the fixed moral catalyst that exposed the true character of everyone around him.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie alone in the classroom — the fixed point that tested Jack, Julian, Via, and every bystander.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Summarizes the book's mechanics before the hosts move to critical examination.
storyboard.addedInformation: The callout generalizes beyond the nature-retreat moment to the book's entire arc.

storyboard.claim: The hosts pause to levy one honest critical examination of the novel itself.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie thinking on the stage — the subject of the analysis; the callout signals a pivot to critique.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After the summary (253), the hosts signal they will challenge the book, not just praise it.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the 'difficult question' is named but not yet stated — the next beats deliver it.

storyboard.claim: The multi-narrator device might let readers feel morally superior without earning it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Charlotte blank-faced holding a book — the reader who feels virtuous just for finishing it; the book icon names the device.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The difficult question (254) is now asked: does the structure make virtue too easy?
storyboard.addedInformation: Charlotte is used here because she is the book's emblem of comfortable moral distance.

storyboard.claim: The reader gets inside Jack's, Via's, Summer's, and Miranda's perspectives — seeing their guilt and eventual redemption.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack and Via thinking side by side — two of the narrators whose inner guilt the reader is given access to.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The virtuous-reading question (255) is now evidenced: we are given too much inside access.
storyboard.addedInformation: Summer and Miranda are not in the cast; Jack and Via represent the multi-narrator access.

storyboard.claim: Julian's perspective is never given — he remains opaque, never understood, never forgiven.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Julian blank-faced and alone — no inner life, no chapter, a closed box.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrast with the multi-narrator access (256): everyone gets a chapter except the villain.
storyboard.addedInformation: Blank expression chosen deliberately — it reads as apathy and absence, not menace.

storyboard.claim: Real life does not punish bullies and reward the kind as cleanly as this book does.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Julian smirking on a street — the bully who in reality often thrives, not loses.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The closed-box critique (257) expands: the whole ending may be too tidy.
storyboard.addedInformation: Julian on street (not school) signals the real-world context the hosts invoke.

callout.text: Julian out, Jack redeemed, August wins

storyboard.claim: In the book: Julian is expelled, Jack is redeemed, and Auggie wins the Henry Ward Beecher medal.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie celebrating on the stage; the trophy icon marks the medal — the book's tidy payoff.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After the 'real life' critique (258), the book's resolution is named as the contrast.
storyboard.addedInformation: The clean three-part resolution (villain out / friend redeemed / hero decorated) is the target of the critique.

storyboard.claim: In the real world the cruelest kids often end up as class president — bullies win.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Julian smirking on the street — the bully who succeeds in real life, not in fiction.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Book's tidy outcome (259) is directly contradicted by real-world evidence.
storyboard.addedInformation: Julian carries the real-world bully reading; his smirk signals ongoing success, not defeat.

storyboard.claim: Does the novel wrap everything so tidily that the reader closes the cover feeling they did a good deed?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Charlotte happy and holding the book — the reader who puts it down feeling morally satisfied.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After the bullies-win real-world contrast (260), the critique focuses on what the neat ending enables.
storyboard.addedInformation: Charlotte's happy face here reads as false satisfaction — the smugness of a reader who thinks reading = acting.

storyboard.claim: Fiction about kindness can become a substitute for action — you cry, you feel good, nothing changes.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Charlotte holding the book with a happy face; the mask icon shows the false virtue she is wearing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The neat-bow critique (261) deepens: comfortable fiction can actively substitute for moral effort.
storyboard.addedInformation: Mask reads as 'pretending' — the reader who performs kindness by reading about it.

storyboard.claim: R.J. Palacio plants Mr. Browne's precept as the counter to the danger of comfortable reading.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Tushman pointing in the classroom — the adult authority figure who delivers the precept as a directive.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After naming the danger of fiction-as-substitute (262), the author's counter-move is introduced.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: Tushman is the principal, not Mr. Browne the teacher; he serves as the nearest adult authority figure in the cast.

storyboard.claim: Choose Kind was never aimed at Auggie — he has no choice. It is aimed at everyone around him.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie sad beside the Choose Kind sign — the person who cannot choose, below the precept that addresses others.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The precept introduced (263) is now reframed: it is not for the boy being stared at.
storyboard.addedInformation: Auggie's sad expression clarifies he is the subject of others' choices, not the agent of his own.

storyboard.claim: Auggie cannot choose a new face — he must endure the stares, whispers, betrayals, and flashlights.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie alone and sad in the forest — the site of one of his hardest endurances.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The Choose Kind reframe (264) is driven home: the precept cannot be for someone with no alternatives.
storyboard.addedInformation: Forest set echoes the nature-retreat threat — the most physical of Auggie's forced endurances.

storyboard.claim: The precept is aimed directly at every bystander — at Jack, at Charlotte, at the neutrals.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Charlotte and Jack side by side, blank-faced; the target icon shows they are the precept's real addressees.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Auggie has no choice (265); the camera turns to those who do.
storyboard.addedInformation: Charlotte's blank expression signals neutrality — the very moral failure the precept targets.

storyboard.claim: Via, Julian's parents, Amos — and by extension, the listener.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Via looking worried — the precept's reach extends past the school to every person who made a choice.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Named characters (266) expand outward to the listener; via is the bridge between book and real world.
storyboard.addedInformation: The target icon echoes beat 266 — the same precept, now aimed all the way past the page.

storyboard.claim: The author demands you examine where you manufacture your own illusions of safety and performative pity.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Charlotte blank-faced holding her notes — the sorting ledger in her hands, aimed at the listener now.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The precept reaches the listener (267); now they are told what to do with it.
storyboard.addedInformation: Charlotte's notes prop makes the sorting-mechanism literal — her paper is the listener's equivalent.

callout.text: Which column on that paper is yours?

storyboard.claim: If you were transported into Beecher Prep's hallways tomorrow — whose column would your name be under?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Charlotte neutral in the hallway; the looseleaf paper icon shows the three-column ledger with the listener's name as the unknown.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The sorting-mechanism demand (268) becomes a specific, personal question.
storyboard.addedInformation: The looseleaf paper icon is the book's moral sorting device made literal — exactly the right moment for it.

storyboard.claim: The three-column list — whose column is your name under?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Charlotte holding her notes with the looseleaf paper icon — the ledger that now includes the listener's name.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The hallway question (269) is specified: it is Charlotte's paper that determines the answer.
storyboard.addedInformation: Repeating the looseleaf icon from 269 reinforces that this is the same sustained final question.

storyboard.claim: The book's final challenge: the listener may be exactly the Charlotte they spent an hour judging.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Charlotte blank-faced in the classroom — the neutral, the person who knew what was right and protected their social standing instead.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The looseleaf paper question (270) delivers its answer: the column most listeners secretly belong to.
storyboard.addedInformation: Blank expression reads as apathy — the neutrality Charlotte embodies and the listener is asked to examine.
